title: Matrix multiplication as composition
summary: Doing one linear transformation after another is again a linear transformation, and its matrix is the product. In S R the right-hand matrix R acts first. Each column of S R is S applied to the matching column of R: follow where î and ĵ end up after both steps. Order matters (S R ≠ R S in general), but grouping does not ((A B) C = A (B C)).
llm_link: Two layers that only multiply by matrices collapse into one matrix (W₂W₁), so stacking them adds nothing. That is why every network puts a nonlinearity between layers. Inside a transformer most of the work is still matrix products, separated by these bends.
key_ideas: Composition: apply R, then S. The result is one linear transformation with matrix S R.
Read products right to left: the matrix closest to the vector acts first, as with f(g(x)).
Column rule: column j of S R = S × (column j of R). Example: S = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] give S R = [[1, −1], [1, 0]].
Order matters: R S = [[0, −1], [1, 1]] is a different matrix. In general A B ≠ B A.
Grouping doesn't: (A B) C = A (B C) (associativity), so any chain of matrices collapses into one.

quiz.q: In the product S R applied to a vector v (that is, S R v), which transformation happens first?
options: S, because it is written first
R, because it is closest to the vector
quiz.explain: S R v means S(R v): R acts on v first, then S acts on the result. Read products right to left, the way the vector experiences them.
Column by column: the left matrix stretches x by 2. First column (0, 1) → (0, 1); second column (−1, 0) → (−2, 0). So the product is [[0, −2], [1, 0]].

quiz.q: R is a quarter turn and S is the shear [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. Is S R equal to R S?
options: Only for vectors on the diagonal
quiz.explain: Rotating then shearing sends ĵ to (−1, 0); shearing then rotating sends it to (−1, 1). Different landing spots, different matrices: order matters.

quiz.q: Why does (A B) C equal A (B C)?
options: Because either way the vector goes through C, then B, then A, in that order
Only when the matrices are square
It doesn't; you must choose one grouping
quiz.explain: Grouping only changes which pair you combine first on paper. The vector still experiences C, then B, then A, so the final motion is the same (associativity).

quiz.q: A network computes y = W₂(W₁x) with no nonlinearity in between. What can you say?
options: It is more powerful than a single layer
It is equivalent to the single matrix W = W₂W₁
quiz.explain: By associativity, W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x: one matrix. Depth only adds power when a nonlinearity (ReLU, GELU, ...) sits between the layers.

problems.title: Multiply matrices column by column
problems.prompt:
Matrices are lists of rows. Write matmul(A, B) that returns the product A B using the column rule: column j of A B is A times column j of B.

matvec from lesson 1.3 and a helper column are included. Build the columns of the answer, then turn them back into rows. If the inner sizes do not match (columns of A ≠ rows of B), raise a ValueError.

S = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]
R = [[0, -1], [1, 0]]
matmul(S, R)   # [[1, -1], [1, 0]]
matmul(R, S)   # [[0, -1], [1, 1]]

tests.name: shear after rotation
tests.code:
out = matmul([[1, 1], [0, 1]], [[0, -1], [1, 0]])
assert out is not None, 'matmul returned None'
assert out == [[1, -1], [1, 0]], f'S R should be [[1, -1], [1, 0]] (i-hat ends at (1, 1), j-hat at (-1, 0)); got {out}'

tests.name: rotation after shear
tests.code:
out = matmul([[0, -1], [1, 0]], [[1, 1], [0, 1]])
assert out == [[0, -1], [1, 1]], f'R S should be [[0, -1], [1, 1]]; got {out}. If you got [[1, -1], [1, 0]], you multiplied in the wrong order.'

tests.name: identity changes nothing
tests.code:
A = [[2, 3], [4, 5]]
assert matmul(A, [[1, 0], [0, 1]]) == A and matmul([[1, 0], [0, 1]], A) == A, 'multiplying by the identity on either side should give A back'

tests.name: rows, not columns
tests.code:
out = matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]])
assert out == [[19, 22], [43, 50]], f'expected [[19, 22], [43, 50]]; got {out}. If you got [[19, 43], [22, 50]], you returned the columns as rows; transpose them.'

tests.name: rejects mismatched sizes

hints: cols = [matvec(A, column(B, j)) for j in range(len(B[0]))]
cols[j][i] is the entry in row i, column j. Rows: [[cols[j][i] for j in range(len(cols))] for i in range(len(A))]

problems.title: Order matters, grouping doesn't (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Use NumPy's @ operator to check the two facts from the video on random matrices.

  • commutes(A, B): return True if A B equals B A (use np.allclose, since floats rarely match exactly).
  • assoc_holds(A, B, C): return True if (A B) C equals A (B C).
  • collapse(layers): given a list of matrices [W1, W2, W3, ...] applied in that order to a vector (W1 first), return the single matrix that does the same job.
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
collapse([W1, W2]) @ x  # same as W2 @ (W1 @ x)
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def commutes(A, B):
    # TODO
    pass


def assoc_holds(A, B, C):
    # TODO
    pass


def collapse(layers):
    # TODO: start from the identity; each new layer acts AFTER the ones before,
    #       so it multiplies on the LEFT
    M = np.eye(layers[0].shape[1])
    return M

tests.name: rotation and shear do not commute
tests.code:
import numpy as np
R = np.array([[0., -1.], [1., 0.]]); S = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
assert commutes(R, S) is False or commutes(R, S) == False, 'R S and S R differ, so commutes should be False'

tests.name: a matrix commutes with itself
tests.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [0., 3.]])
assert commutes(A, A), 'A A equals A A, so commutes(A, A) should be True'

tests.name: associativity on random matrices
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A, B, C = rng.normal(size=(3, 3, 3))
assert assoc_holds(A, B, C), '(A B) C should equal A (B C) up to rounding; are you using np.allclose?'

tests.name: collapse two layers
tests.code:
import numpy as np
W1 = np.array([[0., -1.], [1., 0.]]); W2 = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
M = collapse([W1, W2])
assert np.allclose(M, W2 @ W1), f'W1 acts first, so the single matrix is W2 @ W1 = {(W2 @ W1).tolist()}; got {np.round(M, 3).tolist()}'

tests.name: collapse a deep stack
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
Ws = [rng.normal(size=(4, 4)) for _ in range(5)]
x = rng.normal(size=4)
y = x
for W in Ws:
    y = W @ y
assert np.allclose(collapse(Ws) @ x, y), 'collapse(Ws) @ x should equal applying the layers one by one'

tests.name: collapse handles changing sizes
tests.code:
import numpy as np
W1 = np.ones((3, 2)); W2 = np.ones((4, 3))
M = collapse([W1, W2])
assert M.shape == (4, 2), f'a 2-vector goes to 3 then to 4 entries, so the single matrix is 4x2; got {M.shape}'

hints: commutes: return np.allclose(A @ B, B @ A)
assoc_holds: return np.allclose((A @ B) @ C, A @ (B @ C))
collapse: for W in layers: M = W @ M
